title: Corvo Coffee: the queue at eight in the morning
prompt: A coffee shop's day is not one market but two. Between seven and ten in the morning, commuters arrive faster than the store can serve them: the queue builds, and some customers look at it and leave without buying. For the rest of the trading day the same store, the same staff and the same machines run well below what they could handle. Our client is Corvo Coffee, a chain of 400 company-owned stores trading 350 days a year, all built to the same format. Corvo's operations director has counted the customers who walk away from the morning queue and believes the chain is leaving money on the pavement; she wants to put one extra barista into every store and has asked us whether that pays. Two things will matter today: at peak the store is capacity-constrained, so a sale it does not make is a sale it cannot recover later that hour, and the cost of a fix must be matched to the hours the fix is actually needed.

exhibits.title: Exhibit 1 — The shape of a Corvo trading day
exhibits.text: 07:00–10:00 is peak: every till and machine is running flat out, the queue is long, and some arriving customers leave without ordering. 10:00–18:00 is off-peak: the same store runs at about a third of what it could serve, and nobody queues. A store trades 11 hours a day, 350 days a year, and Corvo has 400 of them.

exhibits.title: Exhibit 2 — One Corvo store, an average trading day (Scenario 1)

rows: Most customers the store can serve per hour
Customers who leave without buying, per hour
Ingredient and cup cost per cup (USD)

exhibits.unitsNote: Every customer buys exactly one cup. Store rent, utilities and the existing staff rota are the same whatever the store sells.
exhibits.source: Store observation study across a sample of 40 stores

exhibits.title: Exhibit 3 — What an extra barista would cost and do
exhibits.text: An extra barista lifts the store's capacity by 30 customers an hour for every hour they are on duty. Corvo can hire them on a peak-only shift of 3 hours at $90 a day, or on a full 11-hour shift at $180 a day. The operations director's proposal is one extra barista in each of the 400 stores, on the peak-only shift, for all 350 trading days.

exhibits.title: Exhibit 4 — Scenario 2: the walk-away count re-measured

rows: Most customers the store can serve per hour
Customers who leave without buying, per hour
Ingredient and cup cost per cup (USD)

exhibits.unitsNote: Changed from Scenario 1: a larger observation study counts 15 walk-aways an hour at peak, not 30. Every other figure is unchanged.

questions.prompt: Let's start with the right structure. What are the three key questions you would need to answer in order to tell Corvo whether to put an extra barista into every store? Please summarise them in 3 lines maximum.

keyPoints: How much demand is genuinely being lost, and is it lost for good or recovered later in the day?
What would an extra barista actually capture — how much extra capacity, in the hours where capacity is the constraint?
What does that capture cost, and does the cost have to be carried for hours when the store is already half empty?
commonMistakes: Reaching for a generic profitability tree (revenue, cost, price, volume) rather than the three questions this decision turns on.
Treating the walk-aways as pure incremental demand without asking whether those customers come back.
Ignoring that the constraint exists for three hours a day and the cost might be incurred for eleven.
Naming six things when the interviewer asked for three.

questions.followUp: Good. The operations team has done an observation study across 40 stores, and the people team has priced the two ways of hiring the extra barista.

questions.prompt: Scenario 1: given the data in the exhibits, what would the operations director's proposal add to Corvo's annual profit across the whole chain? Please give your answer rounded to the nearest whole number, without further explanation or working.
questions.answerFormatNote: Give your answer in USD per year, rounded to the nearest whole number (for example 1111 or 123456 or 500885), without further explanation or working. If the proposal loses money, enter the answer with a minus sign, for example -250000.

idealAnswer.workedSolution:
Contribution per cup = $4.50 − $1.50 = $3.00.
Where is the constraint? Only at peak: the store serves 120 an hour against a ceiling of 120, and 30 customers an hour leave. Off-peak it serves 40 against a ceiling of 120, so nothing is lost there and an extra barista adds nothing.
An extra barista adds 30 customers an hour, exactly the number walking away, for the 3 peak hours: 30 × 3 = 90 extra cups a day.
Extra contribution = 90 × $3.00 = $270 a day. Peak-only shift = $90 a day. Uplift = $180 a day per store.
Across the chain: $180 × 350 days × 400 stores = $25,200,000 a year.
keyPoints: The uplift exists only in the hours when capacity binds; the other eight hours contribute nothing.
Match the shift to the constraint: the peak-only barista costs half as much as the full shift and captures exactly the same cups.
Rent, utilities and the existing rota do not change, so they are not part of this decision.
commonMistakes: Applying the 30 walk-aways an hour across all 11 trading hours and answering $126,000,000 — averaging away the very peak the case is about.
Pricing the full 11-hour shift at $180 and answering $12,600,000 when the constraint lasts three hours.
Using the $4.50 price rather than the $3.00 contribution, and answering $44,100,000.
Loading a share of store rent onto the extra cups, when rent does not change.

questions.prompt: Please explain briefly the reasoning behind your answer to the previous question, in 3 lines maximum.

keyPoints: The store only loses sales where it is capacity-constrained, which is the three peak hours; off-peak there is spare capacity and no queue.
An extra barista adds 30 customers an hour, which is exactly the walk-away rate, so the capture is 90 cups a day valued at contribution, not price.
The cost is matched to those hours — a peak-only shift — and then scaled by 350 trading days and 400 stores.
Fixed store costs are untouched by the decision and stay out of the calculation.
commonMistakes: Explaining the multiplication without saying why only the peak hours count.
Describing the gain as revenue rather than contribution.
Not mentioning that the barista's capacity uplift happens to match the walk-away rate — the assumption the next questions will test.

questions.followUp: Understood. The people team confirms the peak-only shift is deliverable: baristas can be recruited for a three-hour morning contract in every market Corvo trades in.

questions.prompt: I'd like to check a couple of the parameters behind that. In Scenario 1, how many extra cups would one store sell on a trading day with the extra barista? Please give your answer rounded to the nearest whole number, without further explanation or working.
questions.answerFormatNote: Give your answer in cups per store per day, rounded to the nearest whole number (for example 1111 or 123456 or 500885), without further explanation or working.

idealAnswer.workedSolution:
The barista lifts capacity by 30 customers an hour, and 30 customers an hour are walking away, so all 30 can be served.
They are only on duty for the 3 peak hours, and only at peak is anyone lost.
30 × 3 = 90 extra cups a day.
keyPoints: Capture is the smaller of the extra capacity and the demand that is being turned away.
Off-peak hours add nothing, because nobody is being turned away then.
commonMistakes: 30 × 11 = 330, applying the walk-away rate to the whole trading day.
Adding off-peak headroom to the answer, when there is no unmet demand off-peak.
Answering 120, the store's hourly ceiling rather than the extra cups.

questions.followUp: Thanks. For reference, the observation study also found that the walk-away rate is stable across the three peak hours — it does not spike in a single half-hour.

questions.prompt: And what would the proposal add to the annual profit of a single store? Please give your answer rounded to the nearest whole number, without further explanation or working.
questions.answerFormatNote: Give your answer in USD per store per year, rounded to the nearest whole number (for example 1111 or 123456 or 500885), without further explanation or working.

idealAnswer.workedSolution:
Extra contribution per day = 90 cups × $3.00 = $270.
Peak-only barista = $90 a day.
Uplift = $180 a day × 350 trading days = $63,000 per store per year.
keyPoints: Days are trading days, not calendar days.
The barista is only paid on days the store trades.
commonMistakes: Using 365 days and answering $65,700.
Forgetting to deduct the barista and answering $94,500.
Deducting the full-shift $180 and answering $31,500.

questions.followUp: That is the store-level picture. Now — the operations director has just come back with a bigger observation study, and the headline number has moved.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is likely to be true for Scenario 2 compared with Scenario 1? Use the data below for your revised calculation. The change is described under the exhibit.
options: The uplift is lower, but the extra barista still pays for itself
The extra barista now loses money in every store
The uplift is unchanged, because the barista's capacity has not changed
There is not enough information to decide

optionRationale: Correct. With 15 walk-aways an hour, the barista's extra capacity of 30 an hour is no longer the constraint — demand is. The store captures 15 × 3 = 45 cups a day, worth $135, against a $90 shift: $45 a day, $15,750 a year per store, $6,300,000 across the chain. Less than a quarter of the Scenario 1 number, and still worth doing.

Wrong, and it is the intuitive answer: halving the walk-aways does not halve the uplift, it cuts it by three quarters, because the barista's cost is unchanged. But $135 of contribution still covers a $90 shift.
Wrong. The barista's capacity is unchanged, which is precisely why it stops being the binding constraint: only 15 customers an hour are available to capture, so half the extra capacity goes unused.
Wrong. Walk-aways, capacity, price, cost and the shift rate are all given. Worth considering seriously where a figure is genuinely missing; here nothing is.
keyPoints: $25.2M becomes $6.3M — a fixed daily cost against a halved capture bites hard.
The constraint has moved from the store's capacity to the size of the lost demand.
The decision does not flip, but the margin of safety nearly disappears: at 10 walk-aways an hour the proposal breaks even.
commonMistakes: Halving the Scenario 1 answer to $12.6M, forgetting the barista's cost does not halve.
Concluding the barista is loss-making because the uplift fell so far.
Re-deriving the whole chain number without noticing only one row changed.

questions.prompt: Please explain in 2 to 3 lines the reasoning behind your answer to the previous question — and say what walk-away rate would make the proposal break even.

keyPoints: The barista's cost is fixed per day while the capture varies with demand, so the uplift falls faster than the walk-away rate does.
At 15 an hour the store captures 45 cups worth $135 against a $90 shift, so it still pays, but with far less room.
Break-even is where 3 hours × w walk-aways × $3.00 = $90, so w = 10 an hour: below that the proposal loses money.
A strong answer notes that the decision now rests on the accuracy of an observation study, and that Corvo could pilot rather than roll out to 400 stores.
commonMistakes: Giving the direction without computing the break-even the question asks for.
Break-even stated per day rather than per hour, without saying which.
Ignoring that the barista's cost is what makes the uplift fall disproportionately.

questions.followUp: That is the right instinct. The operations director accepts the pilot logic, and would like to pressure-test the Scenario 1 number before committing.

questions.prompt: Back to Scenario 1. Which of the following statements, if true, would change the chain-wide annual uplift you calculated? Select all that apply.
options: Baristas cannot be hired on three-hour contracts in this market, only on full 11-hour shifts at $180 a day
The walk-away rate at peak is 45 customers an hour, not 30
Store rent is a fixed monthly amount and does not vary with sales
Ingredient and cup costs will rise by $0.30 a cup next year
Two in every five customers who walk away at peak come back to the same store later the same day

optionRationale: Changes it. The same 90 cups are captured, but the shift now costs $180 instead of $90, so the daily uplift halves to $90 and the chain-wide figure falls to $12,600,000. The capture is unchanged; only the match between cost and constraint is broken.

Does not change it. The extra barista only adds 30 customers an hour of capacity, so 30 an hour is all that can be captured whatever the walk-away rate is. More lost demand is a reason to consider a second barista — it is not a change to this calculation.
Does not change it. A cost that is the same whether or not the barista is hired does not belong in an incremental calculation at all.
Changes it. Contribution falls from $3.00 to $2.70, so the daily capture is worth $243 against the $90 shift and the chain-wide uplift falls to $21,420,000.

Changes it, and it is the one most often missed. Those customers were never lost — serving them at peak simply moves a sale Corvo would have made anyway. Only three in five of the 90 cups are incremental: 54 cups worth $162, an uplift of $72 a day and $10,080,000 across the chain.
keyPoints: Test each statement against your own terms: capture, contribution, cost, and whether the sale is genuinely incremental.
A capture capped by the barista's own capacity does not move when demand rises.
Recovered demand is not lost demand — this is the difference between a sales uplift and a sales transfer.
commonMistakes: Picking the higher walk-away rate, which feels obviously material until you check what the barista can actually serve.
Picking the fixed rent because it is a large number in the store's P&L.
Missing the returning customers, which is the only statement that questions whether the demand was lost at all.

questions.followUp: That last point has changed the operations director's mind about how to measure this. Separately, the property team has asked about a different way to catch the same commuters.

questions.prompt: Corvo is considering a small kiosk format for commuter locations. Choose the five pieces of data that, when combined, would allow us to estimate the profit one kiosk would generate over its whole life. Treat every cup a kiosk sells as an incremental sale for the chain.
options: Upfront cost to build and fit out the kiosk
The kiosk's useful life, in years
Cups the kiosk can sell per year
Average contribution per cup over the kiosk's life
Fixed running cost per year, averaged over the kiosk's life
Customers passing the kiosk site in the busiest hour of the day
Share of kiosk customers who would otherwise have bought at a nearby Corvo store
Rent the kiosk site would command on the open market

optionRationale: Needed. Lifetime profit is what the kiosk earns less what it cost to build.
Needed here. Unlike a set of year-by-year projections, these figures are averages, so nothing tells you how many years to run them for. The life has to be picked separately.
Needed. Annual volume is what the average contribution is applied to.
Needed. Contribution, not price: the cups cost something to make.
Needed. A kiosk carries rent, utilities and staff whether or not it is busy.

Not needed for this number, and it is the most tempting wrong answer in a case about peaks: busiest-hour footfall is what sizes the kiosk's equipment and rota, but lifetime profit runs on annual volume, which another option already gives you.
Not needed. The question tells you to treat every cup as incremental, which is exactly what this figure would otherwise let you adjust for.
Not needed as a separate input. Rent is real money, but it is already one of the fixed running costs per year — take it twice and you understate the kiosk by its own rent.
keyPoints: Lifetime profit = years × (cups per year × average contribution per cup − fixed cost per year) − upfront cost.
That expression consumes exactly the five selected items and nothing else.
Whether the life is a separate input depends on how the other figures are expressed: averages need a life, year-by-year projections already carry one.
commonMistakes: Taking busiest-hour footfall because this case has been about peak demand throughout, when what the formula needs is the year's volume.
Taking the cannibalisation share despite the assumption stated in the question.
Dropping the useful life by analogy with cases where the projections are given year by year.

questions.followUp: Thanks. One last thing before we write this up for the CEO.

questions.prompt: Your BCG project leader has asked you what could stop the extra-barista uplift from ever showing up in Corvo's accounts, even if the arithmetic is right. Could you share your thoughts in 3 to 4 lines?

keyPoints: The bottleneck may not be the barista: if the constraint is the espresso machine, the till, or the space to queue, a second pair of hands captures nothing.
Serving 30 more customers an hour at peak may slow service for everyone, and the walk-aways could return at the same rate.
Recruitment and rota reality: three-hour morning contracts are hard to fill and turn over fast, and unfilled shifts mean the cost lands without the benefit.
Measurement: the walk-away count came from an observation study, and the two studies already disagree by a factor of two.
Whether the extra sales are genuinely new or moved from later in the day, or from the Corvo store two streets away.
commonMistakes: Listing generic retail risks with no link to how the uplift was calculated.
Missing the possibility that the barista is not the binding constraint, which is the risk that would void the whole number.
Repeating the walk-away measurement point alone when the question asks for a range of reasons.

closing: That is everything I wanted to cover. You found the constraint, priced the fix against the hours it is actually needed, watched the case nearly collapse when the demand estimate moved, and then separated sales that are new from sales that were only ever moved. Thank you — the CEO sees this on Monday.
